title: Sharing audiences with Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford
summary: At the Savoy his band and Webb's alternated; with Lunceford he shared a 10,000-person Philadelphia show.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Back to the Chick Webb Band and the Andy Kirk Band and the Claude Hopkins. You know, we've been mixing some of these names as we went along as we did just a minute ago with Buddy Johnson and some others. How did this work in terms of your sharing the same audience? Did you, for example, share the same audience as the Chick Webb Band?

Oh, yes. We did, especially when we were together at the Savoy cause when Chick would go on, he'd go and play 45 minutes. And then, when he'd take his break, I was on for 45 minutes. So, that's the same audience. They were standing right in front of the band all the same time. And the people, they liked, they liked us both. And, they showed it. They enjoyed it. Cause, take for instance, Ella Fitzgerald, at the time she was nothing but a kid at the time. Sixteen or 17 years old, I believe. And, we got her out of the Harlem Opera House

contest there, I believe.
So, we all shared the same audience
together. Sometimes, we were by ourselves. But,
the same people would come there. I'm just
speaking of the Savoy alone. And then if we go
to the theaters, we used to get the same respect
from the people that you'd get from other bands.
I did the same thing with Jimmie
Lunceford. We, I had a tune out called "Do You
Wanna Jump Children". That was in 1939, too, I
believe. Jimmie Lunceford had a tune out, that
was a big seller for me at that time. Jimmie
Lunceford had a tune out "For Dancers Only".
And then we both, they booked us both in Phila-
delphia at the same time in the Convention Hall.
This guy wanted a big crowd, so he got it then.
They had us both on stage together. This
fellow, Durese Dupree, that was the agent, the
booker. And, he brought this 10,000 people. I
haven't seen a crowd like that for, since, you
know, in one day cause that was kind of early.
And, we was up there and that excited us both,
both bands. He did his big number and I did
mine. Then, we alternated during the rest of the night. Then, we did tunes together. And then I had to put on my big show.

Jimmy Lunceford's band and my band, we were something like brothers, like we called it, cause although he was there maybe 1 or 2 years before me, he treated us like brothers. You know. We looked for each other. We used to run across each other on the road during one night stands, across our path.
So, we were kind of close. We were very close.
